extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in scholarly communication, librarians, journal editors, and open-access advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Identify journals operating with an overlay model and evaluate their characteristics (policies, repositories, peer-review, licences, indexing, metrics, publisher types, article volumes, languages, costs, and service providers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of overlay journal
rubrics_metrics.description: For peer-reviewed original articles, the journal (1) mandates or encourages the submission of preprints to an external OA repository and (2) hosts the final published articles in an external OA repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that the exact definition may vary (Brown, 2010) but these two criteria are used for inclusion in the study. The overlay journal links to repository-hosted final versions and provides issue/volume/DOI metadata. Variants include retrospective uploads of articles after conversion to overlay model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion: currently accepting submissions and active status
rubrics_metrics.description: Only journals currently operating with the overlay model and accepting manuscript submissions were included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals that previously operated as overlays but are no longer active (not accepting submissions) or that have transferred to other publishing models were excluded from the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: platform-hosted venues and non-matching models
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform-based venues that host preprints and final articles on their own platform (e.g., F1000 Research, PeerJ, Scipost, Open Research Europe), software journals pointing to GitHub, rapid review/annotation venues (e.g., Rapid Reviews COVID-19), and services that do not meet both overlay criteria were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer Community In (PCI) and SSRN eJournals were discussed as partial matches but excluded because they do not always host final articles on an external repository or impose other constraints (e.g., fees, non-OA hosting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission / preprint availability policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the journal mandates, encourages, or requires submission of preprints to external OA repositories prior to journal submission, or accepts direct submissions not available as preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study 25 of 34 journals (74%) only accepted submissions of preprints already available in repositories; 9 (26%) also accepted direct submissions but often encouraged repository upload. Most journals operated with the principle of open submissions (none were invite-only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting of final published articles in external repository
rubrics_metrics.description: The final published article versions are hosted in an external open-access repository (as part of the overlay model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes linking from the journal to the repository-hosted final version, and in some cases retrospective uploads after conversion. Hosting on the journal’s own proprietary platform disqualifies the venue as an overlay under the study definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review type (open vs blind vs mixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of peer-review process: blind throughout, open peer-review (publishing reviewer reports), both (author/editor/author choice), or not explicitly defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals publishing review reports (named or anonymous) were classified as operating with open peer-review. In the sample 29 (85%) were blind, 1 (3%) openly published review reports, 2 (6%) accepted both open and blind, and 2 (6%) did not define their process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author and reader charges (APC / access fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the journal requires article processing charges for authors or access fees for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of the investigated journals required fees from readers or authors; one journal had a voluntary APC. Thirty (88%) explicitly stated a no-fee policy; three (9%) lacked information (assumed no fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript source repositories used
rubrics_metrics.description: Which preprint repositories are allowed/used as manuscript sources for submissions (e.g., arXiv, HAL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: arXiv and HAL were the most frequent: 26 (76%) allowed arXiv submissions and 17 (50%) allowed HAL. Figure 3 in the article maps repositories by discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service provider / overlay platform
rubrics_metrics.description: The overlay journal service provider used to enable linking and compiling repository-hosted documents into journal issues (e.g., Episciences, Scholastica, PubPub).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episciences was the most common (20 journals, 59%), Scholastica used by 8 (24%). The study excluded venues that host everything on their own platform (F1000 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher type classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorisation of the organisation behind the journal: individual/group of academics, scientific society, commercial, university/research institute, professional non-commercial publisher, or university press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study used Laakso and Björk (2013) definitions. If a journal website lacked publisher information, the editorial board was interpreted as the publisher. In the sample 18 (53%) were published by groups of academics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing / copyright of published content
rubrics_metrics.description: The licence under which published content is released (Creative Commons variants, arXiv variants, unspecified licence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most journals (25, 74%) used Creative Commons licences. Breakdown: CC-BY 16 (47%); licence not defined 7 (21%); CC-unspecified 5 (15%); CC-BY-SA 3 (9%); CC-BY-NC-SA 1 (3%); arXiv variants also present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing status (DOAJ, Scopus, Web of Science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the journal is indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), Elsevier’s Scopus, or Clarivate’s Web of Science Core Collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing was checked by ISSN and title searches. About one-third were indexed in DOAJ (10, 29%), Scopus (11, 32%), and Web of Science (10, 29%). Newer journals (founded after 2017) were often not yet eligible for some metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal metrics assessed (national rankings and citation metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of qualitative national journal rankings (Finnish Publication Forum, Danish Bibliometric Research Indicator, Norwegian Register) and quantitative citation metrics (Journal Citation Indicator, 2‑year Impact Factor, IF rank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nordic rankings were used to classify journals into levels (FPF/DBRI: 1=basic,2=leading,3=top; NRSJP: 1=basic,2=leading). JCI/IF data were collected for 2020. The study notes inconsistencies across Nordic rankings and that some IFs derive from pre-conversion eras.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISSN presence and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the journal has ISSN numbers and cross-checking ISSNs with Ulrich’s periodicals database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISSN numbers were identified on journal websites and verified with Ulrichsweb. In the sample 29 of 34 journals (85%) had an ISSN.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication languages and geographic base
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages accepted for publication and the country base of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All 34 journals accepted English; eight also accepted French, fewer accepted German, Spanish, Italian. Many journals were based in France (15), with others across US, Canada, UK, Germany, and several other countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article volume measurement and time-series (2018–2021)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of articles published under the overlay model per journal for years 2018–2021; used to identify largest journals and trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When journals were indexed in Scopus, Scopus article volumes for 2018–2021 were extracted; otherwise article counts were manually tallied from journal webpages. Figures show field-level outputs and top five journals by volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Year of establishment and conversion to overlay model
rubrics_metrics.description: Date of journal establishment and date (or year) when the journal started publishing based on an overlay model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study distinguishes born-overlay journals vs converted journals. Visualisations map establishment and conversion years; nearly half (16, 47%) started as overlay journals in 2020 or later. Some journals retrospectively uploaded older articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and repository trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether repositories used by overlay journals perform robust backups, plan for long-term archival, and transparently communicate sustainability aspects (trustworthiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors emphasise the need for repositories to communicate sustainability to ease assessment of trustworthiness and reference the TRUST principles (Lin et al., 2020). Risk: self-managed journals may vanish without preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open data / transparency of collected data
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the study's collected data are openly archived for reuse and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors deposited the collected dataset as open data with DOI (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6420517) to facilitate future research and replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation rule for missing publisher info
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journal website did not include publisher information, the editorial board was interpreted to publish the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational rule affects classification of publisher type for journals that are informally run by academics; used to categorise 53% of sample as published by groups of academics.
